hpi_details: A 35-year-old male presents to the clinic with progressive bitemporal hemianopsia and headaches. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks his blurred peripheral vision and headaches are caused by severe eye strain and an outdated glasses prescription from staring at dual computer monitors.
concerns: He is worried that he is gradually going blind and will lose his driver's license, leaving him unable to commute to his job.
expectations: He hopes to be referred to an eye specialist and get a prescription for stronger corrective lenses today.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Pituitary Adenoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Pituitary Adenoma: Brain MRI, hormone panel, transsphenoidal resection, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Pituitary Adenoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Craniopharyngioma without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Rapid vision loss.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

history.answer: I came in because I've been having trouble seeing things off to both sides, and I keep having these dull headaches.
It started about two months ago very gradually, and my side vision has been getting progressively worse since then.
It affects both of my eyes on the outer sides; when I cover one eye at a time, I still can't see things on the outside edge.
No, it does not come and go. The vision loss is constant throughout the entire day.
The center of my vision is clear, but it feels like I'm wearing blinders because the outer side edges are completely missing.
Straight ahead is clear whether I look close up or far away, and getting new glasses last month didn't help at all.
No glare or halos around lights, but driving at night is scary because I cannot see other cars in my peripheral vision.
No, I haven't seen any floating specks, bright flashes of light, or dark curtains over my eyes.
No, I haven't experienced any double vision.
No, my eyelids haven't been drooping, and I have no trouble chewing or swallowing food.
No, my eyes don't hurt at all, even when I look around, and they haven't been red.
It is a constant, dull aching pressure across my forehead and temples, worse in the morning, but my temples are not tender to the touch.
No weakness or numbness in my arms or legs, and no slurred speech or dizziness.
No, I have never had any head injuries or trauma to my eyes.
No, I don't have diabetes or high blood pressure, and my last routine checkup was normal.
No history of heart conditions, palpitations, or problems with the arteries in my neck.
No, I don't have severe nearsightedness, glaucoma, or cataracts, and I've never had eye surgery.
No, I do not take steroids, hydroxychloroquine, or any antibiotics for tuberculosis.
No one in my family has glaucoma, macular degeneration, or unexplained vision problems.
I've bumped into door frames and pedestrians on the street recently, and I had to stop driving because changing lanes was too dangerous.
I've been feeling unusually worn out and fatigued lately, and my sex drive has dropped noticeably over the last few months.
My ring and shoe sizes are the same, and I haven't had nipple discharge, voice changes, or sensitivity to cold or heat.
I thought my glasses prescription had just worn off or that staring at two computer monitors all day was straining my side vision.
I'm terrified that I'm losing my eyesight completely and won't be able to drive my car to work anymore.
I have always been healthy and have never been diagnosed with any chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries or stays in the hospital.
I don't take any regular prescription medications, just an occasional acetaminophen tablet for the headaches, which doesn't help much.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines or foods.
No, I have never smoked in my life.
I drink alcohol socially, usually one or two beers every couple of weeks.
I work as an office accountant and live at home with my wife.
Both of my parents are healthy in their 60s, and there's no family history of brain tumors or endocrine disorders.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Patient appears well-nourished, alert, and oriented, with normal coarse facial features and no signs of acromegaly.
Sclerae are non-icteric and conjunctivae are pink without injection or discharge.

Visual acuity is 20/20 in both eyes, but confrontation visual field testing reveals a clear bitemporal hemianopsia; pupils are equal, round, and briskly reactive with no afferent pupillary defect, and fundoscopic exam shows sharp optic disc margins with no papilledema.
Extraocular eye movements are intact without diplopia, nystagmus, or ptosis, and facial sensation and movements are symmetric.
Normal muscle bulk and tone with 5/5 strength throughout all upper and lower muscle groups bilaterally.
Intact light touch and pinprick sensation bilaterally without dermatomal sensory deficits.
Normal finger-to-nose testing, smooth rapid alternating movements, and steady tandem gait.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, mobile on swallowing, and free of palpable nodules.
